name: Positive psychology and well-being approaches
summary: These approaches build well-being, strengths, positive emotion and meaning, rather than only reducing symptoms. They are useful adjuncts and relapse-prevention tools, not first-line treatment for moderate or severe depression.

keyConcepts.meaning: Well-being understood as more than the absence of illness, often described through positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning and accomplishment (the PERMA framework).
Personal qualities such as kindness, curiosity, perseverance or humor that a person can recognize and use more often in daily life.
Positive emotions widen attention and thinking in the moment and, over time, help build lasting personal and social resources.
Deliberately noticing, extending and sharing positive experiences, rather than letting them pass unnoticed.
Well-being therapy works on autonomy, environmental mastery, personal growth, positive relations, purpose in life and self-acceptance.

viewOfProblem: Distress narrows attention to threats and losses, and people with depression or anxiety may struggle to notice, take in or build on positive experiences. Low well-being is also a risk factor for relapse. Problems are not denied; the approach adds attention to what is going well and to the person's strengths and resources.
viewOfChange: Change comes from regular practices that increase positive emotion, engagement and connection, such as noticing good things, using strengths in new ways, gratitude, kindness and savoring, and, in well-being therapy, from monitoring moments of well-being and the thoughts that cut them short. Over time these build resources that protect against relapse.
therapistStance: Warm, encouraging and collaborative, with genuine interest in the client's strengths. The clinician acknowledges pain first and avoids forced positivity, and tailors practices to what the client values and finds natural.
sessionShape: Check in on mood, measures and what went well since the last session.
Review the week's practice, including any barriers or mixed feelings it raised.
Explore a strength, a positive experience or a dimension of well-being in depth.
Choose and plan a practice for the week that fits the client's life.
Close by naming one thing the client wants to notice or do more of.
goalStyle: Goals describe well-being actions and experiences: for example, write down three good things on five evenings a week for a month, or use a named strength in a new way at work twice a week. Pair them with symptom goals where depression or anxiety are present. Write each goal with the client in their own words.
progressMarkers: Completion of well-being practices, recorded by the client.
Client ratings of well-being, meaning and positive emotion.
Symptom measures such as the PHQ-9 alongside, to make sure symptoms are not being missed.

missingTechniques.name: Positive psychotherapy (Rashid and Seligman)
missingTechniques.note: A structured 14-session program built on strengths and positive resources; overview only.

models.name: Positive psychology interventions
models.summary: Brief practices such as gratitude, three good things, strengths use, kindness and savoring, delivered individually, in groups or online.
models.evidence: A 2021 meta-analysis of 347 studies found small-to-medium effects on well-being and on depression, anxiety and stress (Carr et al., 2021); an earlier meta-analysis of RCTs found smaller effects (Bolier et al., 2013).

models.name: Well-being therapy
models.summary: Fava's short-term therapy that uses a well-being diary and cognitive work on the six dimensions of psychological well-being, often after other treatment to prevent relapse.
models.evidence: A 2021 meta-analysis of 17 RCTs found that sequential psychotherapy after acute antidepressant treatment, in every trial a form of CBT and in some combined with well-being therapy, lowered the risk of relapse or recurrence (Guidi and Fava, 2021); trials of well-being therapy on its own are few.

evidenceSummary: Positive psychology interventions improve well-being and modestly reduce depression, anxiety and stress (Carr et al., 2021, 347 studies), with smaller effects in stricter RCT-only analyses (Bolier et al., 2013). Well-being therapy is used within sequential CBT-based strategies that lower relapse risk after acute treatment for depression (Guidi and Fava, 2021). No major guideline recommends positive psychology interventions as a stand-alone treatment for depression or anxiety.
bestFit: Building well-being and resilience after symptoms have improved, as part of relapse prevention.
Mild low mood or stress, alongside other support.
Clients who respond well to a strengths-based, hopeful framing.
As an adjunct to first-line treatment for depression or anxiety.
cautions: Not a first-line treatment for moderate or severe depression; use it alongside guideline-recommended care.
Forced positivity or gratitude can feel invalidating, especially after loss, trauma or injustice; acknowledge pain first and let the client choose practices.
Some practices, such as gratitude letters, can stir up difficult feelings; check in afterward.

Low mood that persists or worsens needs review. If thoughts of death or self-harm come up, follow your risk procedures and review crisis options: in the US call or text 988; elsewhere, the local emergency number or findahelpline.com.
whenToRefer: Moderate or severe depression, or no improvement in symptoms: offer or refer for first-line treatment.
trainingNote: Brief positive psychology practices can be used within general training. Well-being therapy and positive psychotherapy have manuals and workshops; no certification is required.

ethicsPrompts.prompt: Practice within your competence: present positive psychology practices honestly as adjuncts with modest effects, not as a replacement for first-line treatment.

culturalNotes: Ideas of happiness, strengths and expressing positive emotion differ across cultures; some value calm contentment or family harmony over excitement or personal achievement.
Gratitude and kindness practices may connect naturally with the client's faith or community traditions; invite those links rather than imposing a secular framing.
Be careful not to suggest that structural hardship can be fixed by a positive attitude.

sources.title: Effectiveness of positive psychology interventions: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Carr et al.)
